meta.title: Raise prices 30% on the existing base?
meta.question: Should I raise prices 30% on existing customers of my $49/month SaaS, or only on new signups?

intake.one_liner: Should I raise prices 30% on my existing customers? $49/mo SaaS, haven't touched pricing in 3 years.

clarifications.q: Roughly how many paying customers and what is monthly revenue today?
clarifications.a: About 1,200 customers, $58k MRR, churn around 3% a month.

clarifications.q: Who does the work if customers push back: you, or a team?
clarifications.a: Me plus two part-time contractors. No sales or support team.

clarifications.q: What do the closest competitors charge?
clarifications.a: Most are $79 to $99. We are the cheapest serious option.

intake.brief: A solo-founded B2B SaaS with 1,200 customers at $49 a month, about $58k MRR, 3 percent monthly churn, and two part-time contractors. Pricing has not changed in three years while competitors sit at $79 to $99. The founder is leaning toward a 30 percent increase to roughly $64 for everyone, including the existing base, and wants to know whether to include existing customers or only new signups.

cast.name: Warren Buffett
cast.tagline: Moats, margin of safety, avoiding ruin

research.claim: Across SaaS benchmarks published in 2024 and 2025, companies that raised prices on existing customers typically saw churn rise 1 to 3 points in the following quarter before settling.
research.source: Aggregate of public SaaS pricing benchmark reports, 2024-2025

research.claim: Grandfathering existing customers for 6 to 12 months while raising list price is the most common pattern among bootstrapped SaaS founders who publish their numbers.
research.source: Indie Hackers and founder public postmortems, 2023-2025

research.claim: Price increases announced with at least 30 days notice and a clear what-you-get-now message see materially lower complaint volume than surprise increases.
research.source: Public pricing-change case studies from SaaS companies

research.claim: No credible source found for a category-specific churn baseline at this price point; the panel is arguing from the founder's own 3 percent figure.

A 30 percent increase on $58k MRR is roughly $17k of additional monthly revenue if churn is unchanged; a 5 point churn spike would erase about $2.9k of base MRR in the first month, so the increase pays for a substantial amount of extra churn.
research.source: Arithmetic on the founder's stated numbers

rounds.title: Opening positions
rounds.chair_intro: One decision on the table: raise prices 30 percent, and whether the existing 1,200 customers come along. Opening positions, your seat's lens, and the fact you most want checked.

turns.speaker: hormozi
turns.text: Three years at $49 while the market sits at $79 to $99 means you have been giving away margin to be liked. Raise it. The math is not close: 30 percent on $58k is $17k a month before a single new customer. Even if churn doubles for a quarter, you are ahead by month two. What I would not do is raise the number and change nothing else. Add one thing people feel, a faster onboarding, a priority support lane, anything, so the message is 'more' not 'sorry.' Existing customers come along after 30 days notice. The question I want answered: how many of your 1,200 would actually leave for a $15 difference when the alternative costs $79?
turns.pull_quote: You have been giving away margin to be liked.
open_questions: What churn spike do SaaS companies typically see after an existing-customer price increase?

turns.speaker: bezos
turns.text: Start with the customer. What gets better for them on the day the price goes up? If the answer is nothing, you are asking them to fund your past under-pricing, and some will resent it even if they stay. That said, this is a two-way door. You can raise new-signup pricing tomorrow, learn for 60 days, and reverse at no cost to the base. The one-way door is touching 1,200 relationships at once with a message you cannot unsend. So: raise list price now, build the mechanism that tells you what happens, then decide about the base with data rather than hope. I want to know the conversion rate on new signups at $64 versus $49.
turns.pull_quote: Raise new-signup pricing tomorrow. The base is the one-way door.
open_questions: Do price increases on new signups alone reduce trial conversion materially?

turns.speaker: buffett
turns.text: I like the business. Twelve hundred customers who have paid you every month for years is a wonderful thing, and I would be careful about teaching them to shop around. The cheapest serious option is a moat of sorts. Being 20 percent cheaper than the field is a reason to stay; being 'about the same' is not. At $64 you lose the moat and keep the smallest support team in the category. My worry is not the $17k. It is that you are spending something hard to rebuild, trust and the habit of not thinking about your bill, to buy a quarter's revenue. If you must, I would rather see you raise on new customers only and let the base age gracefully. What is the real churn after increases like this?
turns.pull_quote: You are spending moat to buy a quarter.
open_questions: What churn spike follows a price increase on an existing SaaS base?

turns.speaker: naval
turns.text: Price is a signal of who you want as a customer. At $49 you attract people who chose you because you were cheap, and those people leave when someone is cheaper. At $64 you start to attract people who chose you because you were good. That is the real reason to do it, not the $17k. The question is whether you have the product and the story to justify being chosen on quality, because if you do not, a price increase just makes you expensive and cheap at the same time. Do it if it is part of becoming the premium option over five years. Do not do it as a cash grab. I want the churn baseline for this category at this price point.
turns.pull_quote: Price is a signal of who you want as a customer.
open_questions: What is a normal churn rate for a B2B SaaS at $50-100 a month?

turns.speaker: blakely
turns.text: Oh my gosh, three years. You have not even asked them. Here is what I would do before this debate goes any further: call ten customers today, tell them you are moving to $64 and why, and watch their faces, or listen to the pauses. You will learn more in those ten calls than from any benchmark. My guess is most will say 'yeah, that is fair,' a couple will grumble, and one will give you a reason you had not thought of. Then raise it, with a hand-written-feeling note that says what you have shipped in three years, because I bet it is a lot and I bet they have forgotten. And give them a tiny gift at the same time. People remember the gift.
turns.pull_quote: Call ten customers today and watch their faces.
open_questions: Do bootstrapped founders usually grandfather existing customers when raising prices?

rounds.chair_summary: The panel splits 2 for, 1 against, 2 conditional. Nobody disputes that $49 is under-priced or that the $17k is real. The split is entirely about the existing base: Hormozi and Blakely would bring them along with a good message, Bezos and Naval want a reason the customer feels, and Buffett thinks the cheapness itself is the moat. Open questions go to the research desk.

rounds.title: Cross-examination
rounds.chair_intro: Research is in. The founder is leaning toward raising on everyone, so the Red Team goes to the panelist most opposed. Reply to someone by name, attack a specific claim, and use the findings.

turns.speaker: buffett
turns.text: Alex says even if churn doubles you are ahead by month two, and the arithmetic is right, which is exactly what worries me. Arithmetic that works on the way up also works on the way down. The research says churn rises one to three points and then settles. Settles where? Nobody knows, because the people who published were the ones it worked for. Here is the case against: you are one person with two part-timers. A hundred angry emails in the same week is not a spreadsheet line for you, it is your whole month, and the product stops improving while you answer them. The moat you have is that nobody thinks about your bill. Raise on new customers, let the old ones be, and you give up nothing you cannot earn back later.
turns.pull_quote: A hundred angry emails is not a spreadsheet line when you are one person.

turns.speaker: hormozi
turns.text: Warren, respectfully, 'nobody thinks about your bill' is not a moat, it is a coma. The research says one to three points of extra churn, and the arithmetic says the increase pays for about six points before you are worse off. That is a margin of safety, your phrase, not mine. On the support flood: the case studies say thirty days notice and a clear 'here is what you get now' message cuts complaints hard. So the founder writes one great email, pre-answers the three objections, and schedules it on a Tuesday. If a hundred people email, a hundred people were going to leave anyway and now you know who they were. I will give you one thing: the new-customers-first sequencing is cheap insurance. Fine. But the base gets the increase within 90 days, not never.
turns.pull_quote: Nobody thinks about your bill is not a moat, it is a coma.

turns.speaker: bezos
turns.text: Sara, I love the ten calls, and I think they are necessary and not sufficient. Ten people who like you enough to take your call are not the 1,190 who do not. What the calls give you is the language for the email, which matters, but the mechanism that tells you the truth is a cohort: raise list price now, watch trial conversion and 60-day retention on the new price, and in parallel send the increase to a random 10 percent of the base with the Blakely note. Then you have a number instead of ten faces. The research on grandfathering says founders usually give six to twelve months. I would give sixty days, because a long grandfather period just means a long time to be anxious about it.
turns.pull_quote: Ten calls give you the language. A cohort gives you the truth.

turns.speaker: naval
turns.text: Alex's math is right and his framing is the problem. 'They were going to leave anyway' is true of any customer under any policy, which makes it useless as a rule. The real question is what story the founder tells, because the research desk could not even find a churn baseline for this category, so we are all guessing about the number and should stop pretending otherwise. What I know is this: if the founder cannot write two sentences about why the product is worth $64 that they would be proud to read aloud, the increase will feel like a tax and it will be treated like one. If they can, the base will mostly shrug. That is the condition. Not a cohort, not ten calls: the sentence.
turns.pull_quote: If you cannot say why it is worth $64 in two sentences, it is a tax.

turns.speaker: blakely
turns.text: Warren, I adore you, and I think you are protecting this founder from a problem they do not have. The scary version in your head is a hundred furious emails. The real version, from every founder I know who did this with a decent note, is a handful of 'fair enough' replies, two cancellations from people who were barely using it, and a surprising number of 'honestly thought you would do this sooner.' Jeff is right that ten calls are not the whole answer, so do ten calls and the 10 percent cohort. But do not hide behind new-customers-only forever. That is the move you make when you are afraid of your own customers, and this founder has been afraid for three years already.
turns.pull_quote: New-customers-only forever is what you do when you are afraid of your own customers.

rounds.chair_summary: Buffett's Red Team case rests on the founder's capacity, not the arithmetic, and the panel largely conceded the sequencing point: everyone now accepts raising new-signup pricing first. The live disagreement is how fast the base follows: Hormozi says within 90 days, Bezos wants a 10 percent cohort first, Naval wants the two-sentence justification before anything, and Buffett still says never. Nobody found a category churn baseline, so the founder's own 3 percent is the only number in the room.

rounds.title: Convergence and vote
rounds.chair_intro: Final positions, what moved you, the condition that would flip your vote, and your scorecard.

turns.speaker: hormozi
turns.text: I moved on sequencing: new signups at $64 this week, base in 60 to 90 days. Jeff's cohort idea is good because it makes the email better, not because the result will be different. My final position is unchanged on the direction, because the numbers do not leave room for a different answer. Three years of under-pricing is a decision you have been making every month by default; make it on purpose this time. What would flip me: a cohort result where more than 8 percent of the test group cancels in 60 days. That would tell me the product has a value problem, not a price problem, and that is a different council.
turns.pull_quote: Under-pricing is a decision you have been making every month by default.

turns.speaker: bezos
turns.text: GO-IF. Conditions: raise list price now, run a 10 percent randomized cohort on the base with sixty days notice and a note that says what shipped, and only roll to everyone if cohort churn stays under about 6 percent over 60 days. Naval moved me on the sentence: the cohort is the mechanism, but the sentence is the input, and the founder should write it before touching anything. Buffett moved me on capacity: schedule the base rollout for a week with nothing else on the calendar. What would flip me is a trial conversion collapse at the new price, because that would say the market disagrees about the value, and the base is not the place to find that out.
turns.pull_quote: The cohort is the mechanism. The sentence is the input.

turns.speaker: buffett
turns.text: I will stay where I am, and I will be honest that I am the only one here. Everyone else believes the churn stays near three points, and they may well be right. I weight the tail. A one-person business with 1,200 customers has one asset: the feeling those customers have about it, and I have watched a lot of good businesses spend that feeling to make a quarter's number. If the founder does this, do it the way Jeff describes, slowly, with a test, with the calendar clear. What would flip me is a cohort where cancellations are under 4 percent and the complaint volume is a trickle. Then I would concede the base was ready and I was protecting a moat that was not there.
turns.pull_quote: I weight the tail. Good businesses spend the customer's feeling to make a quarter.

turns.speaker: naval
turns.text: GO-IF, on one condition that nobody can check for the founder: that this is the first step toward being the premium option, not a one-time grab. If it is, then $64 is the wrong number, because they will be at $89 in three years and should write the roadmap for that now. If it is not, Warren is right and they should leave the base alone. Sara moved me that fear of the base is the real issue here, and that is worth naming. The scorecard reflects that the upside is bigger than $17k and the fit depends on whether the founder wants this game. What would flip me: the founder admitting they do not actually want a premium product.
turns.pull_quote: $64 is the wrong number if you will be at $89 in three years.

turns.speaker: blakely
turns.text: GO. Ten calls this week, the note goes out with the cohort next week, and the whole base in 60 days unless the cohort screams. I moved toward Jeff's cohort because it is cheap and makes the note better, and I love that Naval made everyone write the sentence. Here is my scrappy add: include a small, real gift with the increase email, a free month of something, a printed sticker, whatever fits, because people forgive a price change when they feel seen. What would flip me: if the ten calls are genuinely bad, like three of ten say they would leave. I do not think they will. I think the founder is about to find out how much their customers like them.
turns.pull_quote: People forgive a price change when they feel seen.

rounds.chair_summary: Two GO, two GO-IF, one NO-GO. The panel converged on a sequence: new-signup pricing now, a 10 percent cohort on the base with notice and a clear note, full rollout in 60 to 90 days if churn holds. Buffett dissents on the base entirely and his dissent is recorded.

hormozi.one_line: Price is the cheapest lever you have. Pull it, in order.

conditions: Raise list price for new signups first and watch 60-day trial conversion
Run a randomized 10 percent cohort on the base with 60 days notice before touching everyone
Roll to the full base only if cohort churn stays under 6 percent over 60 days
bezos.one_line: Two-way door first, one-way door only with data.

buffett.one_line: Raise on new customers. Leave the base alone.

conditions: Write the two-sentence reason the product is worth $64 before sending anything
Decide whether this is step one toward premium pricing; if yes, plan the next increase now
naval.one_line: Do it as the first step to premium, or do not do it.

blakely.one_line: Call ten customers, send the note with a gift, stop being afraid.

decision.headline: Raise it, in order: new signups now, a 10 percent cohort next, the base in 60 to 90 days.
decision.summary:
The council agrees the price is wrong and the $17k a month is real. The disagreement was never about whether $49 is too low; it was about the 1,200 existing relationships and a solo founder's capacity to absorb a bad week. The panel converged on a sequence that keeps the reversible moves first: list price to $64 for new signups this week, then a randomized 10 percent of the base with 60 days notice and a note that says what shipped in three years, then everyone if cohort churn holds under 6 percent.

**Write the sentence first.** Naval's condition carried the room: if the founder cannot say in two sentences why the product is worth $64, the increase will read as a tax. Blakely's ten calls produce that sentence. Buffett dissents on touching the base at all and his case, that the 'nobody thinks about the bill' habit is the moat, is the thing to watch for in the cohort data.
conditions: Raise list price for new signups first and watch 60-day trial conversion
Write the two-sentence reason the product is worth $64 before sending anything
Run a randomized 10 percent cohort on the base with 60 days notice before touching everyone
Roll to the full base only if cohort churn stays under 6 percent over 60 days

actions.text: Call ten customers and tell them the new price and why. Write down the exact words they use.
Change new-signup pricing to $64. Do not announce it; just change it.
Write the increase email: what shipped in three years, what is new now, the date, and one small gift.
Send it to a random 10 percent of the base with 60 days notice. Clear that week's calendar for replies.
Roll to the full base, or stop, based on cohort churn and complaint volume.

kill_criteria: Cohort cancellations exceed 6 percent within 60 days of notice, against the 3 percent baseline
Trial-to-paid conversion at $64 falls more than a third below the $49 rate over 60 days
More than 10 percent of the cohort writes in to complain, regardless of whether they cancel

dissent.speaker: buffett
dissent.text: I am the only one voting no, and I may be wrong. But a one-person business with 1,200 customers has exactly one asset, which is the feeling those customers have about it, and I have watched a lot of good businesses spend that feeling to make a quarter's number. Raise on new customers and let the base age gracefully. If the cohort shows cancellations under 4 percent and a trickle of complaints, I will concede I was protecting a moat that was not there.
